The Rule of Change of Addends

ArithmeticInvariantsLogic

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: Explore why changing one number in a sum changes the answer by exactly the same amount.
How to play: Press + or − beside either addend. Watch the dots and the total change together.
Look for the math

Starting from 1 + 1 = 2, nudge one of the ones. The total moves by the very same step — every time, for every starting pair.

What the dots show

The first row of dots is the first addend, the second row is the second addend, and the last row puts them together. Moving a dot from the first row to the second leaves the last row untouched; adding a dot to either row adds exactly one dot to the last row. This is what addition means for groups of objects.

Why the total follows

If the first addend grows by k, the new sum is (a + k) + b. By associativity this equals (a + b) + k: the old sum plus k. The same argument works for the second addend. That is the entire rule of change of addends, and it is why the applet never needs to store the answer — it recomputes it from the two numbers each time.

What the check found

The logic test tries every pair of addends from 0 to 100 and every allowed nudge, confirming that the total moves by exactly the amount the chosen addend moved, that the three dot rows count to the three numbers, and that the sum agrees with an independent calculation. The applet's own about-box calls itself "Dot patterns & modular arithmetic", a leftover from another applet; this page is about the change of addends.

Can you change one addend and keep the total fixed? What would the other addend have to do?
